story_text.value:
Cloakroom is an open-source privacy tool that masks secrets and sensitive data from AI agents. It swaps real values for placeholders, then swaps them back to the originals locally.

I was trying to build a full on local LLM setup on my machine, but the local models were not up to the mark (at least, not yet). I ended up building a hybrid setup, with the cloud for planning and local models for execution. I realized I needed a privacy layer so cloud models could not access sensitive data, and I built Cloakroom.

It runs on your machine, it’s cross-platform, and it works with Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex CLI.

story_text.value:
I built Crewplane because I wanted more control and flexibility over how my coding agents work together, and a way to trace what happened.

Workflow is defined in Markdown, and Crewplane runs the nodes defined in the workflow using native coding CLIs such as Codex and Claude Code. So the control is back to you: different workflows for different tasks with different models, what they depend on, and how they run (parallel or sequential or both). Every input, intermediate output, log, manifest, and final result is preserved on disk so you can trace a run after the fact.

Workflows can be reused and composed into larger pipelines, and interrupted workflows can be resumed. There is no vendor lock in, and it’s easy to adapt your workflows for various tasks - research, design, implementation, debugging, deployment, anything that works as structured procedures.

Give it a try and adapt your own workflows, there is a built-in Mock CLI so you can just try the workflow syntax and composition without worrying about costs (no model calls). Any feedback or suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Open source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/crewplaneai/crewplane

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I’m John. I’m excited to share something I’ve been working on for a long time and releasing today: AppTraction, a native Mac app for Apple’s App Store Connect.

I spent 10 years as an engineer at Apple working on macOS and iOS, and the last 8 as an indie developer with 20+ apps on the App Store for myself and clients. AppTraction is the tool I wish I’d had when I started building my own apps.

Most iOS and Mac devs that I talk to agree that Apple’s App Store Connect website is slow, confusing, and buggy. There’s a lot of useful data there, but the clunky site makes it really hard to make sense of. AppTraction brings your sales, analytics, ratings, and reviews to your Mac, and then tells you what matters.

I won’t get into all the app features here, you can find those on the website, but it has some interesting capabilities so please check them out.

Some background on the development process: AppTraction started as a straight port of the App Store Connect website to a native Mac app, and for about two months that’s all it was. Having the analytics data cached and instant was fantastic, but it still required a lot of time and expertise to interpret. At that point I tried connecting Claude directly to the structured data via MCP, and the results were pretty astonishing. Right away it caught that Apple had featured my apps in Australia and the UK, which I’d been totally oblivious to. It also explained that my bread baking app’s sales decline (which I knew about) wasn’t a problem with the app at all, but a recurring seasonal slump, which is evidently typical for baking apps in the summer. That’s when the Insights tab, which now looks for things like these automatically, became the main view of the app.

The AI runs on your existing Claude Code or Codex subscription (or OpenRouter). AppTraction uses the CLI you already have, so there are no API fees and no API keys to expose. A bundled, read-only MCP server lets the AI query your data with real tools rather than a pasted dump, and you can point your own AI at it.

Privacy: AppTraction was designed with privacy in mind from day 0 so there’s no account, no ads, and your App Store data is stored only on your Mac. AI requests go straight from your Mac to your AI provider, under your account, and my servers never see them.

Pricing: It’s free for 14 days, then $6.99/month, $39/year, or $99 lifetime. Requires macOS 26 Tahoe or later. (No ASC key handy? There’s a demo app with sample data to play with.)

I’d love to hear any feedback, and happy to answer questions of course.

story_text.value:
Inspired by Karpathy's HackerTube, I wondered what was buried in "What are you working on?" thread comments. I wanted to see what changed, and who was still at it years later. So, I built this site to answer some of those questions.

A couple of things you can do: type in your idea and see who already tried it, look up your username and see what you were working on in 2020, see who’s been working on the same thing for a decade, or what founders posted before they had a company.

I built it using Claude Code. Claude Sonnet read all 20,982 top-level replies and pulled out a name, description, topic and how AI was involved. One finding is that AI went from 1% of answers in 2009–11 to 33% this year.

A few limits of the result: labels are model output, and I only spot-checked them. The HN thread only went monthly in 2024, so early years are thin. If I’ve mislabeled your project, or you’d rather not be included, please tell me.

If you’ve been posting here for years, I’d love to hear what happened to those projects.

title.value: Show HN: Search 17 years of "What are you working on?"

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Leon. I built Thrum which runs the coding agents you already use and gives them functionality to work as a team.

It started as an open source project late last year but then in May I went crazy and added a ton of features. I was using it every day to build itself and to do everything else I needed to do with agents. As I found limitations in what agents can do, I added features to the product.

The basic features were all there in a month or so and then I wrapped it all in the GUI. By this time the agents had sent over 200,000 messages and the whole thing fell over and I then had to spend 3 weeks fixing all of the cludge the agents had built and optimizing everyting. That got the performance to less then 1 second for any command and now the database I use has over 700,000 messages and the performance is still great.

Its full cloud infrastructure for your agents but is not cloud based. It connects over git, LAN, Tailscale, and soon SSH. The only data I see is the licensing part. I built it to run fully local so you choose where to spend your tokens.

It does everything I need to do any of the projects I work on so I just need to talk to one coordinator and they handle everything. I also created a steward ( like the steward on a ship ) and they watch all of my coordinators and important agenst like brainstormers and act as my steward to keep me up to date and I can tell it what to respond. It bugs me on telegram if I ignore it :)

The story: https://thrum.team/blog/launching-thrum-pro.html Give it a try-for free here: https://thrum.team Happy to answer any questions you have here.

Leon
